KEY MESSAGE 1...Rain will develop tonight and continue Thursday, 
with colder air then allowing for the rain to mix with and change to 
wet snow Thursday night through Saturday.

Latest ensemble means including the NBM have trended a little colder 
and a little higher on QPF, especially for Thursday night. Given 
this trend, increased snowfall totals a little with this update 
across higher terrain, especially for the Tug Hill Plateau and 
western Adirondacks.  

A series of shortwaves diving south out of Canada will carve out a 
deep longwave trough over the Great Lakes by Thursday, with a 
broad/deep closed low evolving and casting a large footprint over 
the eastern CONUS and southeast Canada by Friday. At the surface, an 
initial low will cross the Ohio Valley tonight before giving way to 
secondary coastal cyclogenesis by late Thursday just off the 
Delmarva. An elongated surface low will then move northeast just 
offshore of the New England coast Thursday night through Friday 
night before reaching the Canadian Maritimes by Saturday afternoon.

Height falls and DPVA ahead of the digging trough will combine with 
increasing frontogenesis and deformation north of the surface low 
track to support rain developing from west to east across the region 
tonight. The rain will be light and spotty initially this evening, 
then increase in coverage and intensity overnight as low levels 
saturate and forcing strengthens. 

Widespread rain will continue Thursday as the surface low passes 
south of the region, and a broad band of frontogenesis and 
deformation persists over northern PA and NY. Precipitation type 
will stay rain in most areas Thursday, but colder air surface and 
aloft will begin to filter into the North Country by afternoon. This 
will likely allow the higher terrain of the Tug Hill Plateau and 
western Adirondacks to change to wet snow, with some very minor 
slushy accumulations possible by evening.

Thursday night, an inverted trough extending north from the 
developing surface low will allow for steady precip to continue 
across Central NY and the North Country. Farther west, the deeper 
moisture and forcing will move away from Western NY, replaced by 
lake enhancement and upslope flow that will still support 
intermittent, light precipitation. Temps aloft and at the surface 
will steadily cool overnight. This will support a change to mainly 
wet snow for the higher terrain in the evening, with the change to 
wet snow then gradually progressing to lower elevations overnight. 
The higher terrain of the Tug Hill and western Adirondacks may see 
several inches of wet snow if the steadier precipitation holds 
through the night. Farther west, only expect very minor slushy 
accumulations across the higher terrain of the Finger Lakes and 
western Southern Tier, with little or no accumulation for lower 
elevations.

Friday through Saturday, chilly northerly flow will continue, with 
the pool of coldest air aloft crossing the eastern Great Lakes 
Friday night through Saturday morning. Moderate lake induced 
instability will continue through the period, but short northerly 
fetch will keep the lake response limited to relatively weak 
multiple bands and lake enhancement. Upslope flow will anchor the 
most persistent precipitation across higher terrain, and also 
enhance QPF amounts to some extent. Expect occasional rain and wet 
snow showers to continue through the period for lower elevations, 
with all wet snow across higher terrain. Precip rates will be light 
most of the time and surface temperatures marginal, so expect 
additional accumulations to be minor and mainly focus across higher 
terrain.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Dry weather will return by early next week, with 
temperatures trending warmer by midweek.

Chilly cyclonic north flow will continue Sunday, although much of 
the deeper synoptic scale moisture and forcing will have exited the 
region. This may still support a few spotty light rain/wet snow 
showers south of the lakes. Dry weather will then return early next 
week as strong high pressure builds east across the Great Lakes. The 
dry weather will likely last most of next week. It will remain 
chilly initially, then a warming trend will develop once the surface 
high moves east of our longitude and height rises/warm advection 
increase aloft.
